message.content:
### Tenant Rights in Texas (as of 2026) | Area | What You’re Entitled To | Key Points | |------|------------------------|------------| | **Security Deposit** | • Must be returned within **30 days** after you move out (unless you and the landlord agree otherwise).
• Landlord may keep money only for: unpaid rent, damages beyond normal wear‑and‑tear, or other costs specified in the lease. | • Landlord must provide an itemized statement if they keep any portion. | | **Habitability** | • Landlord must keep the unit in a safe, livable condition (plumbing, heating, electrical, structural integrity). | • If the landlord fails to maintain habitability, you can withhold rent, repair & deduct, or terminate the lease. | | **Notice Requirements** | • For non‑payment of rent: **3‑day notice** (unless the lease says otherwise).
• For lease termination: **30‑day notice** (or 60 days if you’ve lived there >1 year). | • Notice must be in writing and delivered personally or by mail. | | **Eviction Process** | • Landlord must file a **Petition for Eviction** in the county court.
• Court will issue a **Writ of Possession** if you fail to comply. | • You have the right to contest the eviction in court. | | **Privacy** | • Landlord may enter only for: repairs, inspections, showing the unit to prospective tenants/buyers, or emergencies.
• Must give **24‑hour written notice** (except emergencies). | • Entry without notice is a violation of your privacy rights. | | **Discrimination** | • Protected under the **Fair Housing Act** and Texas’ own anti‑discrimination laws.
• Landlords cannot discriminate based on race, color, religion, sex, national origin, familial status, disability, or source of income. | • If you suspect discrimination, file a complaint with the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD) or the Texas Commission on Human Rights. | | **Lease Terms** | • Lease must be in writing if it’s longer than one year.
• Any changes to the lease must be agreed upon in writing. | • Oral agreements can be enforceable but are harder to prove. | | **Rent Increases** | • No statutory limit on how much a landlord can raise rent, but increases must be in writing and given at least **30 days** notice. | • Some cities (e.g., Austin) have local rent‑control ordinances; check local ordinances. | | **Repair & Deduct** | • If the landlord fails to fix major problems, you may repair them yourself and deduct the cost from your rent (but only if the repair is necessary for habitability). | • Keep receipts and document the problem. | | **Right to a Written Lease** | • Even if you signed a verbal agreement, you can request a written lease. | • A written lease clarifies responsibilities and protects both parties. | | **Legal Remedies** | • You can sue for breach of contract, damages, or unlawful eviction.
• Small claims court handles disputes up to $20,000. | • Consider mediation or arbitration before litigation. | --- #### Quick Checklist Before Moving In 1. **Get a written lease** – read it carefully; ask questions about deposits, maintenance, and notice periods. 2. **Document the unit’s condition** – take photos or videos of existing damage. 3. **Ask about the security deposit** – confirm the amount, where it will be held, and the return timeline. 4. **Know your local ordinances** – some cities have additional tenant protections (rent control, eviction moratoria, etc.). #### Resources | Resource | What It Offers | How to Access | |----------|----------------|---------------| | **Texas Property Code** | Statutory tenant‑landlord law | Online at the Texas Legislature website | | **Texas Attorney General – Consumer Protection** | Guidance on security deposits, lease disputes | ag.texas.gov | | **U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD)** | Fair housing complaints | hud.gov | | **Texas Commission on Human Rights** | Discrimination complaints | tchr.texas.gov | | **Local County Clerk’s Office** | Filing for eviction, small claims | Visit or call your county clerk | | **Legal Aid Organizations** | Free or low‑cost legal help | Search “legal aid Texas” online | --- ### Bottom Line As a Texas tenant, you have clear rights regarding security deposits, habitability, privacy, and fair treatment. If a landlord violates these rights, you have legal avenues—notice, repair‑and‑deduct, or court action—to protect yourself. Always keep written records, communicate in writing, and seek professional advice if you encounter disputes.
